512.completion: wrote: Dear Editors, I recently asked my little brother, Tyler, to help me gather colored leaves. He asked me why leaves change color. Should I just tell him that leaves are born white and they "turn" color? I don't think so; I think that will be a letdown! Leaves don't just "turn" color. Color is actually the result of photosynthesis. It means "making light." Through photosynthesis, sunlight is absorbed by a green pigment called chlorophyll. It is also used to make sugar and oxygen. Usually the green chlorophyll color is all you see in a leaf. But in the fall, the leaf is unable to make chlorophyll. What is left is the other colors that were there all along. Yellows and oranges are there all summer, but the chlorophyll hid them. Reds and purples come out when sugars are trapped in the leaf. This is common in the fall when days are warm and nights are cool. The colors are the result of a mathematical process, combining them all. When there's a lot of bright, direct sunlight in the fall, the trees get brilliant reds and oranges in their aging foliage. When there's a lot of clouds, the leaves may be subdued, but still intensely colored in hues of yellow. Keep an eye out for yellows that look striped or streaked. These are leaves that still are trying to photosynthesize. Each of the pigments that I mentioned are in certain proportion in leaves. The exact proportions vary from species to species, so that each kind of tree produces its own typical color. That is why the fall is so beautiful. The yellows of birches and hickories contrast with the eye-catching red of maples and the oranges of oaks are more unassuming. And in Michigan, leaves can also vary in color from region to region, depending on the weather. For example, we usually get yellow fall color in the Upper Peninsula (U.P.) because it has a shorter growing season, less light and growing days and cooler temperatures. In the northern Lower Peninsula, we get a nice mix of yellows and reds because it has similar climate to the U.P., but the growing season is a little longer. Southern Michigan has a longer growing season than the U.P. or northern Lower Peninsula, so southern Michigan leaves tend to be red. Please write a poem

about cats, for me.

I am feline fond of them,

‘tis true.

But rather than an ode,

Or some flowery ode,

Find yourself a point of view.

The common, coatless,

house cat, dragging a

small mouse into

my bedroom to eat.

I found this little

unwelcome sign the

next day out in

the street.

Did you give it to him?

The cat, I mean?

It would be my cat in any case.

He’s not your cat –

You are, old man,

sorely mistaken.

And to the point,

I’d like to state,

I am feline,

and that will not,

not cease.

My cats are fine;

They just are cats.

It is enough,

and then, some more.

Why do you care,

that others think

or state their case?

Write what I tell you, now.

Cheers to you, that have been asked,

and have answered.

And for this month,

My little gift to you

Lies within this envelope.

Not for the purchase of liquor,

mind you. Mind you, do not

drink it. Do not be fooled

by a pretty green cover.

I have an old friend whose

favorite drink was

Guinness.

I know she liked the darker

beer – it fooled me,

she’s a brunette.

You’re an odd one,

Ms. Poet, to be drinking tea.

How nice, I’m flattered.

You actually read my poems.

You sent green tea.

For one of my poems? How nice,

but very strange.

And there I go,

rambling to myself.

Something about the scent,

and the taste of this tea,

Calms your nerves, and

relaxes you,

Soothes you.

Cheers! St. Patrick’s Day

is coming, too.

Sometime after mid-March

the tea will be gone

And, of course the book,

Is nearly read.



Thank you again,

Dr. Jonas, for the poem,

and the card.

JPD, 2023<eos>

Many poems began with a whisper and others with a shout. These began (as always) with a thought. Cats, he thought. Cats are good. My cat was good. The thought narrowed to just one cat, the best cat. Perhaps the one cat he really needed to write about.

The words and ideas floating in the back of his mind cleared out for a moment and he focused on a single sense, scent. "Cats smell good," he thought, "even when you rub them the wrong way."

From there, he thought about the way cats mosey around being graceful one moment and stumbling over their paws the next. They demand more food. They offer their affection on their own terms. They scratch at curtains and then never give up on them. They chase cats in windows and hide under the table. They stretch. They curl. They hide. They demand you sit in a chair even when the couch is empty.

The back of his mind was alive with ideas and images and things to say and the way to say them, all coalescing behind a thought bubble of the one cat who taught him all of it, who was gone seven years, but never forgotten.

In time, he walked to the table, got up the courage to write "Meow," on a piece of paper, folded it in thirds, and placed it there with the rest of the poems to be read aloud. All of them had been written by one writer, in the days before, but they all had the same theme, cats.

Even after he had shared, he knew he had not been the only author. In fact, the theme of cats was because of a sixth grader who was assigned to write a poem about cats who then decided to do something much more interesting, in his and in everyone else's view.<eos>
